steps.say: This is the B C D Trip Intelligence app, running on Databricks. Every new version of a booking flows through it in real time.
Across the top: in the last five minutes, thousands of booking versions arrived, but only about fifteen percent changed anything that matters. The rest are routine re-saves from the booking systems.
Each version is compared to the one before it and classified in well under a hundred milliseconds, from event to decision, at B C D's peak rate of one hundred versions a second.
On the right, the hourly batch lane is minutes behind. Same data, two consumers, each at the latency it actually needs.
Below is the live feed of significant changes, tagged with what changed and which business rules fired. I'll open a schedule change.
Here is that one booking's full history. Version one created the trip. The next versions were noise, so they're greyed out.
Then the airline cancelled the flight and moved the traveler to a new one forty five minutes later. That's the schedule change, and both rules fired on it.
Every version is compared to the one before it. None are skipped. This is the track changes service that runs in Lambda today, as one step in the stream.
Now the rules engine. An analyst types a rule in plain English.
If a traveler's email address changes, notify the profile sync service.
type: If a traveler's email address changes, notify the profile sync service

steps.say: The A.I. turns it into a Jason Logic rule, the same rule format B C D already uses, with a plain English explanation of what it does.

steps.say: Approve, and it's live. No code and no deployment. The stream picks up the new rule within seconds.
And the hits counter for the new rule is already climbing.
Finally, the traveler. When the airline changes a flight, the same event becomes a notification on their phone. Your flight moved. Accept, or rebook.
The traveler accepts, and the answer is written straight back. The same action is also built as an event for A W S EventBridge, for any downstream service to pick up.
Real time where it matters, batch where it's enough, and rules owned by the business. All on one platform.
